t: Careers and Pathways in Digital Technology
l: Hello and welcome to Mr Butler's Digital Technology podcast. I'm Aoife.
And I'm Conor. Today's episode is for Year 10, and the topic is Careers and Pathways in Digital Technology.
Which is perfect timing, because Year 10 is when you choose your GCSEs.
We'll cover why digital skills matter in nearly every job, six big tech career areas, the tech industry here in Northern Ireland, and the routes from GCSE to apprenticeships and university.
Then the practical bit: the skills employers want, building a portfolio, your online reputation, writing a CV, diversity in tech, and making your own careers plan.
Right, let's start with a picture. When you hear tech job, what do you imagine?
Somebody in a hoodie, typing green code in a dark room, probably eating cold pizza.
Exactly. And that picture leaves out almost everyone. Nearly every job now uses digital technology.
Farmers in Fermanagh use sensors and apps to track their animals' health. Nurses update electronic patient records on tablets.
Rugby coaches analyse match video and GPS data. Mechanics plug in a diagnostic computer to find engine faults.
So digital skills, meaning the abilities to use, understand and create with technology, help you whatever job you end up in.
Employers also love transferable skills. Those are skills you can carry from one job to another, like problem solving and communication.
And automation, where computers do tasks people used to do by hand, still needs people to set it up, check it and improve it.
Now, the six career areas. Number one: software development.
A software developer, also called a programmer or software engineer, plans, writes, tests and improves programs.
They work in cycles: plan, design, develop, test, then release and refine, and round they go again. Just like you do in class.
They also read user stories. A user story sounds like this: as a pupil, I want to see my homework on my phone, so that I don't forget it.
And these days developers often use generative AI tools to suggest code. But the golden rule is: read it and test it, because AI can be confidently wrong.
Number two: cyber security. A cyber security analyst watches systems for signs of attack, like a login from another country at three in the morning.
They make sure data is protected with encryption, like the HTTPS padlock on websites, and they train staff to spot phishing emails.
Number three: data science and AI. A data scientist cleans up messy data, looks for patterns and builds AI models that make predictions.
And a big part of that job is checking the model is fair, and not biased against some groups of people.
Number four: networking and cloud. Network engineers build and look after networks, from fibre cables to Wi-Fi.
Cloud computing means storing data and running software on servers in data centres, reached over the internet.
And here's a link to your KS3 learning: data centres use a lot of electricity, and water for cooling. So cloud engineers have to think about sustainability.
Number five: web, U X and games design. U X stands for user experience.
A U X designer uses user-centred design. That means asking who a product is for, not just whether it works.
They test with real users, refine the design, and check accessibility, following guidelines called W C A G, so people with disabilities can use it too.
Games designers plan the rules, levels and story of a game, then test it until it's fun and fair.
And number six: IT support. These are the people who set up laptops, reset passwords and keep everyone's tech working.
It's a really common first job in tech, and lots of people move on from it into networking or cyber security.
Pause and test yourself. Ciara loves drawing and always notices when an app is confusing. Which career area might suit her?
Web, U X and games design. She cares about design and about users, which is exactly what a U X designer does.
Let's come closer to home. You don't need to leave Northern Ireland for a tech career.
Belfast is known around the world for software and especially cyber security.
A 2023 snapshot from Queen's University Belfast counted about one hundred and twenty-four cyber security firms in Northern Ireland, employing about two thousand seven hundred and fifty people.
And about eighty-five percent of those firms were in Belfast. Though remember, numbers like that change every year.
Tech jobs aren't only in tech companies, either. Hospitals, councils, banks, manufacturers, schools and small local firms all need tech staff.
And then there's hybrid working, which means splitting your week between the office and home.
So someone living near Enniskillen could work for a Belfast company and only travel up a couple of days a week.
The downside? It's harder to learn from experienced colleagues when you're not sitting beside them.
Now, qualifications. At E R G S, GCSE Digital Technology follows the C C E A specification, Route B, Programming.
That's three units. Unit one, Digital Technology, is a one hour exam worth thirty percent.
Unit four, Digital Development Concepts, is a one and a half hour exam worth forty percent.
And Unit five, Digital Development Practice, is a controlled assessment worth thirty percent. You build your own programmed solution in class.
Quick maths challenge. If you get sixty percent of the marks in Unit five, how many percentage points of the whole GCSE is that?
Eighteen. Unit five is worth thirty percent, and sixty percent of thirty is eighteen.
After GCSE, there's A level Digital Technology, also from C C E A, with four units, including an application development project.
And after A levels, two main routes: university, or an apprenticeship.
University usually means three or four years studying something like computer science, software engineering or cyber security, often with a placement year.
An apprenticeship is a real, paid job with training built in. In Northern Ireland, ApprenticeshipsNI covers levels two and three.
And Higher Level Apprenticeships cover levels four to seven, from foundation degree right up to master's level.
You need to be at least sixteen, work at least twenty-one hours a week, and it takes at least two years.
And there's no higher education tuition fee to pay. South West College, which has a campus right here in Enniskillen, offers them in computing.
In England they call it a degree apprenticeship. Here, the same idea is a Higher Level Apprenticeship at level six.
And please don't believe the myth that apprenticeships are a second choice. Places with top employers can be really competitive.
So what do employers actually look for? Technical skills, yes, but also problem solving, teamwork, communication and resilience.
Resilience means keeping going when things go wrong. Which, if you've ever had code refuse to run five minutes before the bell, you've practised a lot.
The trick is not just to say you have a skill, but to prove it. Use the STAR method: Situation, Task, Action, Result.
And in the Action part, say I, not we. The employer wants to know what you did.
Pause and test yourself. What do the four letters of STAR stand for?
Situation, Task, Action, Result. Well done if you got all four.
Next, your portfolio. That's a collection of your best work that shows what you can do.
School projects, things you've made at home, coding clubs like Code Club or CoderDojo, and competitions.
Speaking of which, big news this year. CyberFirst, which many of you have heard of, has become part of a bigger programme called TechFirst.
The TechFirst Girls Competition is for teams of up to four girls, and in Northern Ireland it's for Year nine.
There's also the Bebras Challenge every November, Capture the Flag cyber puzzles, hackathons, and Sentinus Young Innovators, Northern Ireland's science and technology fair.
One warning: never put copied code, or code an AI wrote, in your portfolio as if it's your own. Always credit your sources.
Now, your digital footprint. That's the trail of data you leave online, and it shapes your online reputation.
Employers and colleges may search your name. And deleting a post doesn't always help, because somebody may have screenshotted it.
So before you post, ask: would I be happy for a future employer to see this?
And use a sensible email address. Skaterboy two thousand and eleven is not going on your apprenticeship application.
Speaking of applications, let's talk CVs. A CV is a short summary of your skills, education and experience, usually no more than two pages.
At your age, a skills-based CV works best. It puts your skills first, each with a piece of evidence.
So instead of good with computers, write something like: built a spreadsheet for the tuck shop with formulas and charts.
Later on, for university, you'll write a personal statement. UCAS now asks three questions, with four thousand characters in total.
Next, diversity. In twenty twenty-five, only about twenty-two percent of IT specialists in the UK were women. That's roughly one in five.
Which is strange, because women have shaped computing from the very start.
Ada Lovelace wrote what's often called the first published computer program, back in the eighteen forties.
And Margaret Hamilton led the team that wrote the flight software for the Apollo Moon missions.
Diverse teams build better products. A team that all thinks alike can miss problems, and AI trained on data from just one group can work badly for everyone else.
So don't let a stereotype choose your GCSEs for you. You don't need to be a maths genius. Practice matters far more.
Finally, your careers plan. Step one, know yourself: what you enjoy, what you're good at, and what matters to you.
Step two, explore: talk to your careers teacher and a Careers Service adviser, and look at real job adverts.
Step three, set SMART targets: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound.
Pause and test yourself. Is get better at coding a SMART target?
No. It isn't specific, you can't measure it, and there's no deadline. Better: go to coding club every week until June.
And step four: get experience, through work experience, volunteering or open days. Then review your plan every year.
Let's recap. One: digital skills matter in almost every job, not just computer jobs.
Two: the six areas are software development, cyber security, data science and AI, networking and cloud, web, U X and games design, and IT support.
Three: Belfast is a big centre for software and cyber security, and hybrid working opens those jobs to people all over Northern Ireland.
Four: at E R G S, GCSE Digital Technology is Route B, Programming, with Units one, four and five. After that, A level, university or a Higher Level Apprenticeship.
Five: prove your skills with STAR, a portfolio and a skills-based CV, and look after your online reputation.
And six: tech is for everyone. Make a SMART careers plan, and change it whenever you need to.
That's it for this episode. Now go and try the quizzes on each page.
Thanks for listening, and good luck with your GCSE choices. See you next time.
